title: Generalization despite memorization capacity
description: Networks that can fit arbitrary labels still generalize from natural data to held-out examples.
bottom_line: Neural networks can memorize random labels, yet trained on real labels they still generalize to new data. Independent studies reproduce this in small models; with random labels, test accuracy stays near chance. Wider networks can lower test error after fitting the training data, though results vary by setup and one comparison found error rising with width. Two claims are contested: that adaptive optimizers such as Adam generalize worse than stochastic gradient descent, and that sharpness (sensitivity to weight changes) predicts generalization. How broadly these findings hold remains open: model scale is rarely reported, and few replications use comparable training conditions.

claims.heading: Networks can memorize random labels and generalize from natural labels
claims.summary: Independent studies support networks’ ability both to memorize random labels and to generalize from natural labels in small-model settings, though their setups vary. In comparisons using both label types, random-label test accuracy is near chance.

claims.heading: Wider networks can lower test error after fitting the training data
claims.summary: Reports describe lower test error after fitting the training data at the studied scales, but shared authors and reused experiments mean the reports are not all independent. The effect depends on setup and width; one tabulated comparison of convolutional networks instead shows test error rising as width increases.

claims.heading: Convolutional networks can generalize better than fully connected networks trained from scratch
claims.summary: Independent groups report a convolutional advantage in image classification, with exceptions across architectures and training conditions; sparse training, which uses fewer active connections, narrows the gap without establishing that connections to nearby inputs cause the improvement. Matching or beating a CNN by starting from weights learned by a convolutional network remains a finding of the original study.

claims.heading: Adaptive optimizers can generalize worse than SGD under limited tuning
claims.summary: A WRN-40-4 study reports lower training loss but worse test accuracy with Adam; a replication reproduces the CIFAR-10 gap but finds the opposite optimizer ranking for a character-LSTM on War and Peace. Tuning only the training schedule removes the gap for VGG on CIFAR-10, while pretraining LLaMA on C4 at the 1B scale favors Adam.

claims.heading: Large batches can hurt generalization under fixed epoch budgets
claims.summary: Several independent groups reproduce a large-batch penalty in image classifiers and language models under fixed epoch or token budgets. Longer training can reduce the penalty, and adapted training recipes sometimes remove it within the same epoch budget.

claims.heading: Dropout lowers test error in some training regimes
claims.summary: Several studies report conditional dropout benefits in fully connected and convolutional classifiers, while very small datasets do not universally rule them out. Hernández-García and König’s study reports results when dropout and weight decay are removed together, with augmentation kept; independent replication remains unestablished.

claims.heading: Lower magnitude-aware sharpness (weight-scaled sensitivity) correlates with smaller generalization gaps in restricted CNN comparisons
claims.summary: A separate study of CIFAR-10 CNNs with low loss supports this correlation using a related estimate of sharpness. How well sharpness ranks models by generalization remains unsettled: it failed in one comparison across depths, and normalized margins—measures of separation from the decision boundary adjusted for model scale—ranked models better in an extended test.

claims.heading: Removing highly memorized examples hurts test accuracy more than random removal
claims.summary: A separate study reports larger losses for partially fine-tuned DistilBERT, using a different method to estimate how strongly each example was memorized. Replication using the original estimation method and image settings remains unestablished.

reading_list.why: Shows that the same unregularized Inception fits natural and random CIFAR-10 labels perfectly while test accuracy differs sharply.
Original unregularized width experiment: test error generally improves after fitting the training data, but not at every width.
Shows incomplete random-label fitting under specified normalization methods and training budgets, leaving longer-training outcomes open.

known_gaps.summary: Incomplete source access, sparse scale information, limited matched replication and unresolved training conditions constrain how broadly these findings can be generalized.
items: Unavailable sources, partially verified findings and figure-only measurements limit completeness. The available evidence cannot establish comprehensive literature coverage.
Model sizes, families and training stages are often unspecified. The evidence does not establish how broadly these findings extend to much larger models.

Independent reproduction of the original experiment removing memorized examples, using its exact estimation method and image settings, remains unestablished. Studies that rank examples using substitute measures of memorization do not resolve that gap.
Apparent disagreements often involve different datasets, metrics, budgets or methods. The available comparisons do not establish additional disagreements under matched conditions.

Optimizer comparisons remain incomplete across architectures, datasets and training budgets. Some reported comparisons also have unresolved source attribution, limiting conclusions about when rankings change.

Some favorable persistence-dropout comparisons remain incompletely represented and lack uncertainty estimates. Ambiguous MentorNet conditions also limit conclusions about its CIFAR-100 dropout comparisons.
Several reported batch-size improvements do not establish where larger batches begin to harm the workload. Their implications beyond an established harmful threshold remain unresolved.
